---
title: "For instructors"
---

Each tool follows the same layout: a question, a few controls with presets, one main chart, number tiles, and a verdict phrased as the legal test. An **Experiments** tab asks students to predict before they reveal the answer; a **Model** tab gives the formulas and sources.

## Using a tool in class

1. Open the tool before the session; the first load downloads the R runtime into the browser.
2. Start from the default preset, which matches the standard textbook example.
3. Ask the room to predict the effect of one change, then move the slider.

## Monopoly and welfare

| Tab | Concept | Teaching point |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Monopoly and deadweight loss | Monopoly Pricing and Welfare; Deadweight Loss (DWL) | The monopolist cuts output; part of the lost consumer surplus is a transfer, the rest is lost to everyone |
| 2 Rent seeking | Rent Seeking; Rent Seeking and the Social Cost of Monopoly | If firms spend resources to win the monopoly, the social cost is the triangle plus part of the rents |

## How many firms?

| Tab | Concept | Teaching point |
|---|---|---|
| 1 The trade-off | Model: Cournot Competition with n Firms; Model: Consumer Surplus and Profits | More firms lower the price but each one duplicates the fixed cost; consumers and society can prefer different numbers |
| 2 Fixed costs and market structure | Fixed Costs and the Optimal Number of Firms; Model: The Optimal Number of Firms | High fixed costs support few firms; free entry can bring more firms than welfare calls for |
| 3 Price competition | Extension beyond the slides: differentiated products, firms set prices | How firms compete after entry decides how many enter: soft competition attracts too many firms, tough competition can leave too few |

## Market definition

| Tab | Concept | Teaching point |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Is a price increase profitable? | Critical Loss; Predicting the Loss: Two Routes; Whole Foods/Wild Oats | High margins lower the critical loss; margins and elasticities must fit together |
| 2 SSNIP step by step | SSNIP Test: Steps; Running Case: Nestlé/Perrier | Widen the candidate market until the price increase is profitable |
| 3 Cellophane fallacy | The Cellophane Fallacy | At the monopoly price the test always fails, so start from a competitive price |

## Concentration and market power

| Tab | Concept | Teaching point |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Shares and markups | Lerner Index; Formal Steps for Indirect Approach; Industry-Wide Lerner Index | In Cournot, L = s/\|η\|; the same shares mean less market power when demand is more elastic |
| 2 HHI and the merger screen | HHI; CR4; What Do Thresholds Actually Mean in Law? | Compute HHI and its change; US presumption vs. EU safe harbour (Heinz/Beech-Nut) |
| 3 Is concentration market power? | High HHI Is Neither Necessary Nor Sufficient | The same HHI gives zero (Bertrand), Cournot or monopoly markups |
| 4 Beyond HHI: diversion and GUPPI | Beyond HHI: Diversion Ratios; From Diversion Ratios to Pricing Pressure | HHI and GUPPI can disagree in both directions; diversion where the competition takes place |

## Technical notes

The tools are R Shiny apps compiled with `shinylive` and run in the browser through WebAssembly (webR). Source code: this repository.
